What the court did next is worth pausing over: instead of treating the two as interchangeable, it slowed down and told two offences apart. I keep returning to that case - Emperor v. John McIver - for a line of Cornish J’s that has aged well. Reading the word ‘entrustment’ as it sat in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC), in the context of criminal breach of trust, he reasoned that property got by a trick is never really entrusted at all; and so, in his words, "the same facts will not constitute both criminal breach of trust and cheating". The two are not shades of one wrong. They are different wrongs, built on different foundations. The root of that reasoning lay in the House of Lords’ decision in Lake v. Simmons, where Lord Sumner had stated that a trick preventing true consent leaves no room for entrusting.
